speaker: Tobias Lütke
title: Tobi Lütke: 21 Years of Building Shopify
question: In e-commerce software engineering, why do teams so often ship bloated architectures that quietly destroy storefront conversion rates?
guest: Why the business model of software is so insane is because zero marginal copying of software is free. The same thing causes a lot of problems for the creation of software because you just don't know how much dead weight is in the system. If you compare this with electrical engineering, there's a very clear cost of manufacturing—the bill of materials dominates the success of a product, so everyone's trained on costing waste out of the system. Software engineering throws away so much of the capability of these powerful machines because it doesn't cost anything. At a certain scale it starts costing, but it's fixed by operations teams getting more servers rather than engineering teams fixing those things. So the consequences of bad decisions are an externality that doesn't accrue back to the engineers who caused it. Computers got much faster and we threw capabilities away making very heavy client-side JavaScript applications that took forever to load, especially in commerce where people visit sites rarely. When you go to a website for the first time, you don't have an up-to-date MacBook with tons of memory like engineering teams—you might have an Android device on a train, sitting there a minute and a half for the store to load. Conversion rate is zero.

points.core: Zero marginal copying hides software waste unlike physical manufacturing costs.
points.note: Accept: software lacks a bill of materials, near-zero duplication cost masks bloat, or no physical unit cost forces efficiency. Do not credit: generic claims that engineers get lazy or ignore technical debt.

points.core: Operations teams absorb inefficiency by adding servers instead of engineers fixing it.
points.note: Accept: infrastructure scaling masks bad code, or performance costs become an externality paid by ops rather than the engineers who caused them. Do not credit: generic mentions of cloud bills or poor cross-team communication.

points.core: Engineers test on fast hardware that masks slow mobile load times.
points.note: Accept: developers use high-end laptops or fast networks that hide latency on low-end phones or spotty connections. Do not credit: generic advice to do more QA testing.

points.core: Infrequent shoppers abandon heavy client-side storefronts before pages finish loading.
points.note: Accept: first-time e-commerce visitors lack cached assets so heavy client-side bundles tank conversion rates. Do not credit: generic statements that slow websites create bad UX.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Mostly because the costs of bloat are invisible to the people creating it, while the benefits are immediate and local.

Each addition looks reasonable on its own: a marketing tag, an A/B testing script, a personalization widget, a reviews plugin, a heavier JavaScript framework. Each has an owner and a business case, but nobody owns the cumulative page weight. Engineers build on fast laptops and office networks, so they never feel what a mid-range phone on a patchy connection feels.

Incentives compound this. Teams are rewarded for shipping features, not for removing them. Architecture choices such as microservices, headless stacks and heavy client-side rendering are often driven by developer experience, résumé appeal, or vendor marketing rather than measured customer need.

The damage is also hard to attribute. A slowdown of a few hundred milliseconds does not trigger an alert; conversion just drifts down and gets blamed on seasonality or ad quality.

That said, "destroy" overstates it for many stores. Speed and conversion are clearly correlated, but the effect size varies, and much-cited figures often come from vendor studies.

The usual fix is performance budgets enforced in CI, real-user monitoring tied to revenue, and a single owner for third-party scripts.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
E-commerce architectures bloat primarily because organizational incentives reward feature velocity, developer ergonomics, and vendor flexibility over real-world storefront speed. Driven by premature scaling and resume-driven trends, teams routinely adopt complex decoupled stacks, heavy client-side JavaScript frameworks, and chatty microservice layers built for hyper-scale applications rather than mostly static retail catalogs. Engineers also build and test on powerful laptops over fast Wi-Fi, masking how severely bundle hydration and network waterfalls stall mid-tier mobile devices on cellular connections, where most shoppers actually buy.

Simultaneously, marketing and merchandising teams independently inject dozens of third-party scripts—analytics, A/B testing, personalization, fraud checks, and payment badges—through tag managers that bypass engineering governance entirely. Because few organizations enforce strict performance budgets or tie real-user monitoring directly to funnel revenue, latency creeps upward in tiny, unnoticeable increments. Every added API hop and vendor tag passes isolated review, yet their cumulative main-thread blocking and delayed interactivity quietly drive shoppers away long before leadership connects falling conversion rates to architectural weight.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Mostly it comes down to incentives, not technical ignorance. Each addition is visible and easy to defend: a personalization widget, an A/B testing tool, a reviews embed, a chat bot, another analytics tag. The cost is spread out and shows up late. No single change makes the site slow. Pages get slower a few hundred milliseconds at a time, and conversion drops gradually in ways that get blamed on seasonality, ad spend or the market.

Several things make this worse. Marketing and other teams can add third-party scripts through tag managers without engineering review. Developers test on fast laptops and office networks, while many shoppers use mid-range phones on patchy mobile connections. Heavy frameworks that render everything in the browser became the default even for mostly static catalog pages. Because of Conway's law, every team ships its own JavaScript and nobody owns total page weight. A/B tests measure whether one feature helps, not what all the features together do to speed.

The research is clear that this matters. For example, Deloitte's 2020 "Milliseconds Make Millions" study found that a 0.1-second mobile speedup raised retail conversions by about 8%. But without enforced performance budgets and monitoring based on real-user data, nobody is held accountable for speed.

models.answer: E-commerce teams often ship bloated architectures because organizational incentives reward visible features and abstract technical elegance over raw storefront speed. Marketing, merchandising, and analytics stakeholders continuously push for personalization widgets, A/B testing scripts, tracking pixels, and third-party plugins, each justified by a plausible local business case while its cumulative cost to page weight and main-thread execution goes unmeasured. Meanwhile, engineering teams frequently over-engineer storefronts with heavy client-side frameworks, microservices, and composable headless stacks to follow industry trends or prepare for hypothetical scale, adding network hops and hydration overhead to every page view. Because developers test on fast laptops and office networks with warm caches, the real-world latency suffered by shoppers on mid-range mobile devices stays invisible. Even when performance degrades, conversion losses happen quietly: users simply bounce before analytics fire or abandon sluggish checkouts without filing bug reports. Without strict performance budgets, real-user monitoring tied directly to revenue metrics, and executive accountability for latency, complexity accumulates unchecked until the architecture itself becomes a silent tax on sales.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Teams ship bloated storefronts because the benefits of each addition are visible and the costs are shared. A personalization widget has an owner and a launch date. A new service promises team autonomy. A tracking script gives marketing a metric it wants. Each decision can make sense on its own, while nobody is accountable for what they collectively do to the shopper’s experience.

The cost shows up when a shopper tries to open a product page or check out. JavaScript competes for the browser’s main thread, service calls add latency, and third-party dependencies introduce more ways for a page to stall. Those costs hit hardest on slower phones and networks, which are easy to miss in a demo or an average. A shopper who leaves before the page finishes loading may never appear in the analytics.

The feedback loop is weak, too. Teams can point to the feature they shipped, while a gradual conversion decline is hard to untangle from changes in traffic, pricing, and promotions.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Teams often ship bloated storefronts because the benefit of each addition is visible to one team, while the cumulative cost is spread across the business. Marketing can measure the reach of a new tracking tag, and merchandising can measure sales from a recommendation widget. Neither metric shows how many shoppers left because the page took longer to become usable.

The damage comes when those additions put more work between a shopper and a purchase. Extra scripts can delay a size selector’s response to a tap. A cart that waits on several services gives one slow dependency the power to stall checkout. Both problems are easy to miss on a developer’s laptop and painful on a midrange phone.

The loss stays quiet because a shopper who leaves rarely generates an error. If teams monitor uptime and each feature’s own metrics, the dashboard can stay green while fewer visitors finish buying.
